title: Deep Read: Attention Sinks, and Why Attention Share Is Not Evidence
summary: A close reading of Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM. The first few tokens soak up a large share of attention, not necessarily because they matter. For anyone measuring how much attention a VLM gives to image tokens, this is required reading first.
body:
There is a rock on the shore, and every time the tide goes out a pool of water collects behind it. The pool is not there because the rock is special. The water simply has to stop somewhere.

This time Snowdrop's spotlight falls on Guangxuan Xiao et al.'s Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (a 2023 preprint, later published at ICLR 2024). It is an engineering paper about streaming deployment, yet along the way it uncovers a phenomenon that is quite unkind to interpretability researchers.

The starting point: slide the window and the model breaks

The authors wanted language models to keep working over an endless stream of dialogue. The most direct approach is sliding-window attention: keep only the key-value cache of the most recent tokens. But they observed that once the very first tokens are evicted from the cache, output quality collapses abruptly, even though what was evicted is only a few semantically unremarkable opening tokens.

Looking at the attention maps, they found that many layers and heads give a substantial share of attention to the first few tokens of the sequence, largely regardless of what those tokens mean.

The explanation: attention has to go somewhere

The explanation is plain and strong:

- Softmax forces each row of attention weights to sum to one. When a head has nothing much to attend to at the current position, the surplus attention still has to be placed somewhere.
- In autoregressive training the initial tokens are visible to every later position, so they are the easiest to train into a dumping ground for that surplus.
- These tokens become attention sinks: they absorb attention not because they carry key information, but because their position means they are always present.

From this, StreamingLLM keeps the key-value cache of the first few tokens permanently alongside the sliding window, which lets the model process very long streams stably without fine-tuning. The authors also propose adding a dedicated learnable sink token during pretraining, so that the dumping behavior is more concentrated and controllable. Note that the method does not extend the context the model can actually use; it only keeps the model from breaking as the window slides.

> A high attention weight may mean only "this is where surplus attention goes", not "this is important".

Why this matters for my question

When studying visual evidence deactivation in long reasoning, a tempting measurement is the share of attention the model gives to image tokens at each generation step, to see whether it falls as reasoning grows longer. This paper tells me that curve can be misread in at least three ways:

1. Sinks contaminate the denominator. If a large share of attention is dumped onto the opening sinks, a change in the image share may just mirror a change in the sink share. Image tokens often sit near the start of the sequence too, which makes the separation more delicate.
2. Images may contain sinks of their own. Some later work has reported sink-like visual tokens in multimodal models that absorb a lot of attention while having little to do with the question. I still need to read those papers closely, but they are enough to suggest that "attention on the image" may itself be a mixture.
3. Attention is not causation. Even an accurate share only says where the model looks, not whether what it saw affected the answer.

So my measurement plan has to change. First identify and exclude sink tokens, then report the share of what remains; and use causal interventions as the primary evidence, such as whether the answer changes when image regions are masked or swapped, with attention share kept as a secondary descriptive signal.

The pool behind the rock does not prove the rock matters. Before reading an attention map, find the places where the water merely stops.
